newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eurotunnel debt restructuring detailed. [CORRECTED 12:20 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel debt restructuring detailed. [CORRECTED 12:20 GMT]

text.p: Shareholders in Channel Tunnel operator Eurotunnel SA/Plc are voting on a complex package to restructure the company's 70 billion francs of junior-ranked bank debt.
The company froze interest payments to its lenders in September 1995 after it saw that annual revenues far undershot its debt service needs and opened talks to refinance its loans.
The rescue plan aims to give the company until 2003 to stabilise its finances, return to profitability in 2005 and pay a first dividend to shareholders in 2006.

The main elements of the debt plan involve a swap of eight billion francs of bank debt for Eurotunnel shares and an issue of various debt instruments which push out the repayment period and bear a lower rate interest than the existing loans.
Eurotunnel's interest charges will fall by 40 percent under the plan, saving it from what executive chairman Patrick Ponsolle calls the "snowball effect" of debt service.
The company paid 5.5 (corrects figure from 3.1) billion francs in interest payments in 1996 and 5.8 (corrects figure from 5.2) billion in 1995.
The plan does not entail cancellation of any debt and leaves intact 45.10 percent of the junior loans which will be repaid between 2005 and 2025.
The terms of the debt restructuring are:

- Banks will swap 11.68 percent of junior debt into equity. Eurotunnel will issue new shares to the banks which will give them 45.5 percent of the equity capital, reducing the holding of the current shareholders to 54.5 (corrects from 44.5) percent. Existing stockholders may also subscribe to shares.

- Eurotunnel will issue equity notes for 11.68 percent of the debt, paying interest of 4.45 percent annually in arrears unti December 31, 2003. If the notes are not redeemed in cash, they will be repaid with share units at a conversion price of 155p on December 31 2003.

- Banks will receive participating loan notes for a further 14.02 percent of the junior debt, paying fixed interest of one percent. The loan notes also allow the lenders to receive 30 percent of a specified measure of annual cashflow. These notes mature in 2040 and replace loans which would have been due for repayment in 2012.

- The debt plan evisages a resettable facility to replace 17.52 of the present debt, with an initial interest rate of 5.28 percent for the French portion and 7.03 percent for the sterling amount, with resetting of the interest rate at regular intervals.

- An issue of resettable bonds will replace 17.52 percent of the existing loans and push out the repayment period to 2050 from 2012. Interest on the bonds will be based on yields on French and British government bonds of equivalent maturity plus a margin of 0.5 percent utnil 2003 and 1.50 percent from 2004.

- If Eurotunnel's cashflow falls short of its debt service needs, it can draw on stabilisation notes to the tune of 1.85 pounds, which pay no interest during the stabilisation period up to 2005. After that, interest will be a margin of 1.25 percent over the interbank rate. These notes can be redeemed from 2018 to 2026 at par. Eurotunnel can convert the notes into shares.

- Eurotunnel will offer its existing shareholders free share warrants on the basis of one warrant for every three share units held, entitling holders to subscribe for one share at any time prior to December 2003.
- Existing shareholders will receive a further series of warrants on a basis of one warrant for every eight shares if the operating licence is extended.

The French and British governments have said they will extend Eurotunnel's concession by 34 years to at least 99 years, if the restructuring plan is approved. They are also asking for an increase in rail freight traffic through the Channel Tunnel and a 25 percent share of net profits from 2052.
If all the warrants were execised, the shareholders would bring their holdings back to 55.5 percent of the capital.
Eurotunnel needs all 174 lenders to approve the debt plan and expects an agreement in the autumn.
-- Pierre Tran, Paris newsroom +331 4221 5452
